screens.title: Unit Testing in Android
screens.subtitle: Local unit tests, test doubles, and testing ViewModel + Repository logic

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn why unit testing is essential for Android development and how to write fast, reliable local unit tests that run on your JVM. Unit tests verify the smallest parts of your app in isolation: a ViewModel method, a repository function, or a utility class. That isolation keeps tests fast and pinpoints failures when code changes. We'll focus on local unit tests that use JUnit and Mockito, and on practical techniques: mocking repository dependencies, synchronizing LiveData with InstantTaskExecutorRule, and controlling coroutines with a TestDispatcher and runTest. You will see concrete examples: a TaskViewModel test that stubs a repository Flow to emit tasks, and a TaskRepository test that verifies interactions with a mocked DAO. Along the way we cover common mistakes — not mocking dependencies, missing InstantTaskExecutorRule, and over-mocking brittle internals — and how to avoid them. By the end you'll be able to set up test dependencies in build. gradle, write tests that observe LiveData deterministically, and verify repository interactions. Think about one class in your project that has clear inputs and outputs; that class will make a great first unit to test.

keyIdea.title: Why unit tests matter
keyIdea.text: Unit tests provide fast, isolated checks of small components so you can detect regressions quickly and refactor with confidence.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Unit Testing in Android
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Unit Testing in Android

Learn how to test the smallest parts of your app quickly on the JVM, isolate dependencies with mocks, and make LiveData and coroutines deterministic in tests.

In this lesson
  • Set up JUnit and Mockito for local unit tests.
  • Isolate ViewModel logic with mocked repositories.
  • Control coroutines and LiveData in tests for determinism.
Explore Key Topics
Local unit tests, mocking dependencies, LiveData and coroutine testing patterns.
Concept Map
Overview
Local Unit Tests
Fast tests on the JVM for pure logic classes.
Mocks & Stubs
Replace dependencies to isolate behavior.
LiveData & Coroutines
Use rules and test dispatchers for determinism.
Repository Tests
Mock DAO and verify delegation.
Coming up
We will step through ViewModel and Repository tests with code examples, test rules, and common pitfalls to avoid.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll gain in this chapter

narration.text: These objectives will guide your practice and testing decisions. First, you will understand the purpose and benefits of unit testing: why small, isolated checks speed up debugging and support refactoring. For example, testing a ViewModel method ensures changes in UI code won't silently break core logic. Second, you will learn to distinguish local unit tests, which run on the JVM, from instrumented tests that require an Android device. This distinction matters because it determines speed and which frameworks you use. Third, you'll learn to set up a local testing environment using JUnit and Mockito so your tests run reliably. The build dependencies and testImplementation configuration keep test libraries out of production builds. Finally, you will start writing effective unit tests for ViewModel and Repository classes, learning how to isolate dependencies and assert behavior. Each objective includes a practical mnemonic to help you remember the test pattern and a verified milestone so you know when you're ready to move on.

screens.title: What is a Unit Test?
screens.subtitle: Definition, purpose, and a practical example

narration.text: A unit test verifies the behavior of the smallest testable part of an application, which can be a single class or method. The defining idea is isolation: a unit test exercises that part while replacing or faking its external collaborators so you measure only the unit's behavior. In Android this typically means testing pure Kotlin or Java classes — ViewModels, Repositories, Use Cases — on the JVM. For example, if a ViewModel exposes LiveData from a repository Flow, a unit test will mock the repository to emit a known list of items and then assert the ViewModel produces the expected LiveData value. The advantage is speed and determinism: because you are not launching an emulator or touching a database, tests run quickly and failures point to the unit under test. A common misconception is that unit tests must test private methods; instead, focus on observable behavior through public APIs. A practical tip is to keep tests readable: clear arrange-act-assert structure, concise test data, and a single assertion focus so the test documents intended behavior. Here's a short checklist to decide what to test: clear inputs and outputs, low external coupling, and logic that is likely to regress. Which small class would you test first in your project?

keyIdea.title: Unit test definition
keyIdea.text: Isolated checks of a single unit's behavior, using test doubles for collaborators to keep tests fast and focused.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › What is a Unit Test?
Definition

A unit test checks a single unit in isolation from its dependencies. It runs on the JVM and focuses on observable behavior through public methods and properties.

Example
Mock a repository to emit a list of tasks; assert the ViewModel's LiveData has that list.
Misconception
Testing private helpers is brittle. Test public behavior instead.
Pro tip
Arrange, act, assert. Keep tests short and focused on one behavior each.
Concrete checklist
  • Does the class have clear inputs and outputs?
  • Can its dependencies be replaced with mocks or stubs?
  • Will the test run quickly on the JVM?
Key Takeaway

Prefer tests that exercise public behavior, isolate external resources, and fail only when the unit is incorrect.

screens.title: Test Doubles: Mocks and Stubs
screens.subtitle: How mocks and stubs isolate behavior and when to use each

narration.text: Test doubles are any object that replaces a real collaborator in a test. Two common kinds are mocks and stubs. A stub provides predefined answers to method calls: it returns fixed data so the unit under test receives expected inputs. For example, when testing a ViewModel that reads a Flow of tasks from a repository, you stub getAllTasks to return a Flow that emits a list you control. A mock not only provides behavior but also records interactions so you can verify that certain methods were called with expected arguments. For instance, verifying that insertTask was called on a repository when the ViewModel saves a new task. Choosing between stub and mock depends on what you need to assert: use a stub to control inputs and a mock to assert interactions. A common pitfall is over-mocking internal implementation details — that makes tests brittle. Prefer verifying public interactions that express the unit's contractual behavior. In Kotlin you can use Mockito-Kotlin or MockK. Keep test doubles simple and focused; they should make the test deterministic and easier to reason about. Test Doubles: Mocks and Stubs means stubs supply responses to calls; mocks also record and verify interactions. use each according to whether you need controlled inputs or interaction checks.. In practical terms, how mocks and stubs isolate behavior and when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Mocks vs Stubs
keyIdea.text: Stubs supply responses to calls; mocks also record and verify interactions. Use each according to whether you need controlled inputs or interaction checks.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Mocks and Stubs
Stub — control inputs
Return fixed data from a dependency so the unit receives predictable inputs. Use stubs when you only need to control behavior, not verify calls.
Example
whenever(mockRepo.getAllTasks()).thenReturn(flowOf(tasks))
Mock — verify interactions
Use when you want to assert a method was called with specific arguments, for example verify(mockRepo).insertTask(newTask).
Example
verify(mockRepository).deleteTask(taskId)
When to avoid mocks
  • Avoid verifying private internal calls; test observable behavior instead.
  • Don't mock too many collaborators; excessive mocking makes tests fragile.
Key Takeaway

Choose stubs to feed input and mocks to assert interactions. Keep tests focused on external behavior.

screens.title: Local Unit Tests vs Instrumented Unit Tests
screens.subtitle: When to use JVM tests and when to run on device/emulator

narration.text: Understanding the difference between local unit tests and instrumented unit tests helps you choose the right approach. Local unit tests run on the JVM and are ideal for pure logic classes that have no direct Android framework dependency: ViewModels, Repositories that operate on domain objects, utility functions, and use cases. They run fast and are suitable for continuous integration. Instrumented tests run on an Android device or emulator. Use them when your code depends on Android framework classes that can't be easily mocked on the JVM — for example, UI components, Resources, or Context-based APIs. Instrumented tests are slower and require device management, so reserve them for cases where the framework behavior itself matters. A frequent misconception is that everything should be instrumented for accuracy; that will slow your feedback loop. Instead, prefer unit tests for logic and use targeted instrumented tests only where the framework is involved. Practically, decide by asking: can I inject or mock the Android dependency on the JVM? If yes, write a local unit test; if not, write an instrumented test. Local Unit Tests vs Instrumented Unit Tests means use jvm local tests for pure logic and instrumented tests only when android framework behavior must be exercised.. In practical terms, when to use jvm tests and when to run on device/emulator. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Test type decision
keyIdea.text: Use JVM local tests for pure logic and instrumented tests only when Android framework behavior must be exercised.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Local vs Instrumented
Local Unit Tests (JVM)
Fast, run on developer machine, used for pure Kotlin/Java logic that doesn’t need Android APIs.
Good for:
  • ViewModels, Repositories that can be mocked
  • Utility classes and use cases
Instrumented Tests (Device)
Run on an emulator or device and required when code uses Context, Resources, or UI components directly.
Good for:
  • UI interactions, Android framework behavior, resource access
Decision guide
  1. Can the Android dependency be mocked or injected? If yes, prefer a local test.
  2. If the behavior depends on Android internals, write an instrumented test.
Key Takeaway

Choose the fastest environment that still gives you reliable verification of the behavior you care about.

screens.title: Set up Local Unit Testing Tools
screens.subtitle: Add JUnit, Mockito, and coroutine testing support

narration.text: Setting up a testing environment for local unit tests is straightforward but important for deterministic results. In your app module's build. gradle you add testImplementation dependencies: junit for the test runner, mockito for creating test doubles, mockito-kotlin for idiomatic Kotlin helpers, kotlinx-coroutines-test for coroutine testing utilities, and core-testing for LiveData utilities. The testImplementation configuration ensures these libraries are available only for tests under src/test. After adding dependencies, sync the project and create a sample test in src/test to validate the setup. A common mistake is adding these to the main implementation configuration, which bloats APKs and causes conflicts. Also remember to include rules and test dispatchers in test classes: InstantTaskExecutorRule for LiveData and a StandardTestDispatcher with Dispatchers. setMain for coroutine code that uses Dispatchers. Main. This process gives you a predictable test runtime and prevents flaky timing-based failures. Finally, run a single test locally to confirm build configuration, then iterate by writing focused tests for ViewModel and Repository logic. Set up Local Unit Testing Tools means add junit, mockito, kotlinx-coroutines-test, and core-testing to testimplementation, then validate with a sample test in src/test.. In practical terms, add junit, mockito, and coroutine testing support. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Setup checklist
keyIdea.text: Add junit, mockito, kotlinx-coroutines-test, and core-testing to testImplementation, then validate with a sample test in src/test.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Testing Setup
Add these dependencies
  • junit:junit:4.13.2
  • org.mockito:mockito-core and mockito-kotlin
  • kotlinx-coroutines-test for coroutine testing
  • androidx.arch.core:core-testing for LiveData
Why testImplementation?
It scopes libraries to the test classpath so they are not packaged into production artifacts and avoid runtime conflicts.
Sample build.gradle snippet
dependencies {
  // Local Unit Testing
  testImplementation 'junit:junit:4.13.2'
  testImplementation 'org.mockito:mockito-core:3.12.4'
  testImplementation 'org.mockito.kotlin:mockito-kotlin:3.2.0'
  testImplementation 'org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-test:1.6.4'
  testImplementation 'androidx.arch.core:core-testing:2.2.0'
}
Key Takeaway

Install test libraries under testImplementation and validate by running a simple test in src/test.

screens.title: Testing LiveData: InstantTaskExecutorRule
screens.subtitle: Make LiveData synchronous in unit tests

narration.text: LiveData is lifecycle-aware and normally posts updates to lifecycle owners, which can cause timing issues in unit tests. InstantTaskExecutorRule is a JUnit rule that forces LiveData to run each task synchronously on the current thread. Add it to your test class with @get:Rule val instantTaskExecutorRule = InstantTaskExecutorRule(). This rule prevents tests that observe LiveData from missing updates or seeing stale values, and it is essential when you use observeForever in tests to capture emitted values. A concrete example: in a ViewModel test you observe allTasks LiveData with observeForever and then advance coroutines; without the rule LiveData updates may not be applied by the time you assert. A common misconception is that Dispatchers and LiveData are unrelated; in practice you often need both InstantTaskExecutorRule for LiveData and a test dispatcher for coroutines to make the whole test deterministic. Always clean up observers when necessary, but observeForever is fine inside tests when used with the rule. Testing LiveData: InstantTaskExecutorRule means for unit tests, use instanttaskexecutorrule to ensure livedata updates execute synchronously and predictably.. In practical terms, make livedata synchronous in unit tests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: InstantTaskExecutorRule
keyIdea.text: For unit tests, use InstantTaskExecutorRule to ensure LiveData updates execute synchronously and predictably.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › LiveData in Tests
Rule example
@get:Rule
val instantTaskExecutorRule = InstantTaskExecutorRule()
This rule forces LiveData to run synchronously and is necessary when using observeForever in tests.
Why it matters
Without it, LiveData updates may be posted asynchronously and assertions can see null or stale values.
Test pattern
  1. Set InstantTaskExecutorRule in the test class.
  2. Observe LiveData with observeForever to capture values.
  3. Advance test dispatchers for coroutines then assert the captured value.
Key Takeaway

Combine InstantTaskExecutorRule with coroutine test dispatchers to make LiveData and coroutine behavior deterministic in unit tests.

screens.title: Testing Coroutines: Dispatchers and runTest
screens.subtitle: Control coroutine execution with TestDispatcher and runTest

narration.text: Coroutine-based code uses dispatchers like Dispatchers. Main inside ViewModel scope. In unit tests you must replace the Main dispatcher with a test dispatcher so coroutines execute under your control. The common pattern is to create a StandardTestDispatcher, call Dispatchers. setMain(testDispatcher) in @Before, and Dispatchers. resetMain() in @After. Use runTest to create a coroutine test scope; it supports suspending test functions and cooperates with the test dispatcher. When your ViewModel launches coroutines, advance the testDispatcher. scheduler until idle or use advanceTimeBy to move virtual time so launched coroutines complete. A concrete example from the TaskViewModelTest uses StandardTestDispatcher and testDispatcher. scheduler. advanceUntilIdle() after observing LiveData to ensure flows are collected. A common mistake is relying on real dispatchers and expecting immediate results. That leads to flaky tests or tests that never finish. Always set and reset the Main dispatcher in test setup and use runTest for suspend testing to get deterministic behavior and clean test isolation. Testing Coroutines: Dispatchers and runTest means use standardtestdispatcher with dispatchers.setmain and runtest, then advance the dispatcher to run pending coroutines deterministically.. In practical terms, control coroutine execution with testdispatcher and runtest. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Coroutine testing pattern
keyIdea.text: Use StandardTestDispatcher with Dispatchers.setMain and runTest, then advance the dispatcher to run pending coroutines deterministically.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Coroutine Testing
Setup pattern
private val testDispatcher = StandardTestDispatcher()

@Before
fun setup() {
  Dispatchers.setMain(testDispatcher)
}

@After
fun tearDown() {
  Dispatchers.resetMain()
}
runTest and advancing
runTest {
  // trigger behavior
  testDispatcher.scheduler.advanceUntilIdle()
  // then assert results
}
runTest gives a test coroutine scope and works with the test dispatcher to control execution deterministically.
Common mistake
Not replacing Dispatchers.Main or not advancing the test dispatcher. Both cause coroutines to remain pending and tests to fail or hang.
Key Takeaway

Always set a test dispatcher as Main and use runTest with explicit advances to make coroutine work deterministic in tests.

screens.title: TaskViewModelTest: getAllTasks example
screens.subtitle: Observe LiveData and stub repository Flow

narration.text: Let's walk through a real test that illustrates many of the patterns we've discussed. The getAllTasks emits tasks from the repository test shows setting up InstantTaskExecutorRule and a StandardTestDispatcher, mocking TaskRepository, stubbing getAllTasks to return a Flow of test tasks, observing the ViewModel's LiveData with observeForever, advancing the dispatcher, and asserting the emitted value. The key steps are: set the Main dispatcher to a test dispatcher so ViewModel coroutines run predictably; configure the mock repository to return flowOf(tasks) so the ViewModel receives known data; observe the LiveData to trigger collection; then advance the testDispatcher. scheduler until idle and assert equality. Finally, verify the repository method was called to ensure the ViewModel interacted as expected. A typical pitfall is forgetting to advance the dispatcher or the InstantTaskExecutorRule, which leaves LiveData empty or tests flaky. This test demonstrates a clear arrange-act-assert flow that keeps the unit isolated and fast. TaskViewModelTest: getAllTasks example means stub repository flows, observe livedata with instanttaskexecutorrule, use a test dispatcher and advance it before assertions.. In practical terms, observe livedata and stub repository flow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: ViewModel test pattern
keyIdea.text: Stub repository Flows, observe LiveData with InstantTaskExecutorRule, use a test dispatcher and advance it before assertions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › TaskViewModelTest — getAllTasks
Test snippet
// snippet from TaskViewModelTest
@get:Rule
val instantTaskExecutorRule = InstantTaskExecutorRule()
private val mockRepository: TaskRepository = mock()
private val testDispatcher = StandardTestDispatcher()

@Before
fun setup() {
  Dispatchers.setMain(testDispatcher)
  viewModel = TaskViewModel(mockRepository)
}

@Test
fun `getAllTasks emits tasks from repository`() = runTest {
  val tasks = listOf(
    Task(1, "Test Task 1", "Desc 1"),
    Task(2, "Test Task 2", "Desc 2")
  )
  whenever(mockRepository.getAllTasks()).thenReturn(flowOf(tasks))

  var emittedTasks: List? = null
  viewModel.allTasks.observeForever { emittedTasks = it }

  testDispatcher.scheduler.advanceUntilIdle()

  assertEquals(tasks, emittedTasks)
  verify(mockRepository).getAllTasks()
}
Explanation
  • Arrange: stub repository.getAllTasks to return a Flow with tasks.
  • Act: observe the LiveData to start collection.
  • Advance: run pending coroutines with advanceUntilIdle.
  • Assert: the observed value equals expected tasks and repository method was invoked.
Key Takeaway

This pattern makes ViewModel tests deterministic and verifies both data flow and interactions.

screens.title: Verifying Interactions: insertTask and deleteTask
screens.subtitle: Use verify to confirm delegation to repository

narration.text: Beyond verifying returned values, many unit tests assert that a unit correctly delegates work to its dependencies. In ViewModel tests this often means verifying that insertTask or deleteTask are called on the repository. The pattern is simple: perform the ViewModel action and then call verify(mockRepository). insertTask with the expected Task object. Because these methods may launch coroutines, make sure to run them inside runTest and advance the test dispatcher so any launched coroutine completes before verification. A concrete example: when viewModel. insertTask(newTask) is called, the test calls verify(mockRepository). insertTask(newTask). This check ensures the ViewModel's responsibility — delegating persistence — holds even if underlying implementations change. A common pitfall is timing: verifying before the coroutine runs will fail. The remedy is to use StandardTestDispatcher and advanceUntilIdle, or to make repository methods non-suspending in the test double if appropriate. Clear arrange-act-assert structure keeps these interaction tests readable and maintainable. Verifying Interactions: insertTask and deleteTask means use verify(mock).method(args) after advancing coroutines to confirm the unit delegates actions to its dependencies.. In practical terms, use verify to confirm delegation to repository. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Verify delegation
keyIdea.text: Use verify(mock).method(args) after advancing coroutines to confirm the unit delegates actions to its dependencies.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Verify insert & delete
Insert test
@Test
fun `insertTask calls repository insertTask`() = runTest {
  val newTask = Task(title = "New Task", description = "New Desc")
  viewModel.insertTask(newTask)
  verify(mockRepository).insertTask(newTask)
}
Delete test
@Test
fun `deleteTask calls repository deleteTask`() = runTest {
  val taskIdToDelete = 1
  viewModel.deleteTask(taskIdToDelete)
  verify(mockRepository).deleteTask(taskIdToDelete)
}
Notes
  • Always verify after advancing the test dispatcher if the method is invoked in a coroutine.
  • Keep the assertion focused on delegation, not implementation order unless order matters.
Key Takeaway

Interaction tests confirm responsibilities: that one component delegates work to another as intended.

screens.title: Testing the Repository
screens.subtitle: Mock the DAO and verify delegation and data flow

narration.text: Repository tests focus on ensuring the repository correctly delegates calls to its data sources, such as a DAO or a remote A P I client. The pattern is simple: mock the DAO, stub its methods to return controlled Flows or values, call the repository method, collect the result, and assert it matches the expected data. For non-suspending delegations like insertTask, simply call repository. insertTask and verify(mockTaskDao). insertTask(newTask). When testing getAllTasks the DAO can be stubbed to return flowOf(tasks) and the repository's returned Flow can be collected to check the same tasks are emitted. The chapter provides a collectForValue helper that launches a coroutine, collects one value from the Flow, then cancels. This ensures tests don't hang collecting continuous flows. The key is to keep the DAO as the only dependency under test and to avoid touching real databases or network calls, which would make tests slow and flaky. Mocking the DAO keeps tests fast and focused on repository behavior. Testing the Repository means mock the dao, stub return values, collect a flow once and assert the repository returns that same data and delegates calls correctly.. In practical terms, mock the dao and verify delegation and data flow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Repository testing pattern
keyIdea.text: Mock the DAO, stub return values, collect a Flow once and assert the repository returns that same data and delegates calls correctly.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Repository Tests
Test examples
val mockTaskDao: TaskDao = mock()
val repository = TaskRepository(mockTaskDao)

@Test
fun `getAllTasks returns flow from DAO`() = runTest {
  val tasks = listOf(Task(1, "Repo Task 1", "Desc 1"))
  whenever(mockTaskDao.getAllTasks()).thenReturn(flowOf(tasks))

  val resultFlow = repository.getAllTasks()
  var actualTask: Task? = null
  resultFlow.collect {
    actualTask = it
    cancel()
  }

  assertEquals(tasks, actualTask)
  verify(mockTaskDao).getAllTasks()
}
Helper note
Collect only the first value from a Flow in tests to avoid hanging. The chapter's collectForValue helper cancels collection after one emission.
Practical checklist
  • Mock the DAO and stub returns for Flows.
  • Collect one value and assert equality.
  • Verify DAO methods are called for mutation operations.
Key Takeaway

Repository tests confirm delegation to data sources while remaining fast by mocking external components.

screens.title: Common Testing Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Avoid flakiness and brittle tests

narration.text: Testing has patterns that lead to brittle or flaky tests if not followed. First, not mocking dependencies turns unit tests into integration tests that use real databases or network calls. Those tests are slower and more likely to fail due to external reasons. Second, forgetting InstantTaskExecutorRule causes LiveData assertions to observe null or stale values. Third, not replacing Dispatchers. Main with a test dispatcher leaves coroutines unexecuted in tests, causing hangs or missing assertions. Fourth, over-mocking internal behavior makes tests tightly coupled to implementation details and hard to refactor. Best practices to avoid these issues include: mock only external collaborators, test public observable behavior, use InstantTaskExecutorRule for LiveData and a StandardTestDispatcher with runTest for coroutines, and keep tests focused with single responsibility. Also prefer small, readable test data and clear arrange-act-assert structure so tests double as documentation. When a class has many dependencies, consider refactoring to smaller units that are easier to test. These measures keep your test suite fast, reliable, and helpful during development. Common Testing Mistakes and Best Practices means mock external dependencies, synchronize livedata and coroutines, and test public behavior rather than internal implementation details.. In practical terms, avoid flakiness and brittle tests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoid brittle tests
keyIdea.text: Mock external dependencies, synchronize LiveData and coroutines, and test public behavior rather than internal implementation details.

content.html:
Caution › Chapter 5.3 › Common Mistakes & Best Practices
Mistake: No mocks
Leads to integration-style tests that are slow and flaky. Mock external systems instead.
Mistake: Missing rules/dispatchers
Without InstantTaskExecutorRule and a test dispatcher you will see timing failures and hanging tests.
Mistake: Over-mocking
Mocking internal details makes tests fragile. Focus on public contracts and behavior instead.
Best practices
  • Keep tests small and focused on one behavior.
  • Use clear arrange-act-assert structure and simple test data.
  • Refactor large classes that require too many mocks into smaller units.
Key Takeaway

Design tests and code together: easier-to-test code is often better-structured code.

screens.subtitle: Three core ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize three core concepts you should carry forward. First, a unit test isolates a single unit of behavior and runs quickly on the JVM; keep tests focused on public behavior rather than private implementation. Second, test doubles such as mocks and stubs let you control inputs and verify interactions; use stubs to provide data and mocks to verify calls, and avoid over-mocking internals. Third, deterministic testing of LiveData and coroutines requires specific test support: InstantTaskExecutorRule for LiveData, and a TestDispatcher with Dispatchers. setMain plus runTest and advancing the dispatcher for coroutine execution. These three ideas — isolation, deliberate test doubles, and deterministic concurrency handling — form the backbone of reliable local unit testing in Android. screens.subtitle: Three quick reminders before you write tests

narration.text: Before you start writing tests, remember these three practical reminders. First, pick a single unit with clear inputs and outputs; that gives clarity to your assertions. Second, mock external dependencies to keep the test fast and focused, and only verify interactions that matter to the unit's contract. Third, handle asynchronous work explicitly: use InstantTaskExecutorRule for LiveData, set the Main dispatcher to a test dispatcher, and advance the dispatcher inside runTest so coroutines complete. Keeping these reminders in mind will make your tests helpful, maintainable, and quick to run.
